lines: Lecture four: how do we classify nanomaterials?
There are many ways: by origin, composition, phase, dispersion, and more. You do not need to memorize those.
The one he will most probably ask is classification by dimension.
The trick is to count the free dimensions: the ones that are still larger than one hundred nanometers.
Start with a bulk block. X, Y and Z are all above one hundred nanometers. Three free dimensions: that is bulk, not nano.
Shrink Z into the nano range, say fifteen nanometers. Two dimensions are still large, so this is a two-dimensional nanomaterial.
A nano film, a coating, a layer or a sheet, like graphene.
Now shrink Y as well. Only one long dimension is left: a one-dimensional nanomaterial.
A nanowire, a nanorod, a nanofiber or a nanotube.
Shrink X too. Nothing is left free, so it is zero-dimensional: a nanoparticle.
Below about ten nanometers, a second change happens. Quantum physics takes over.
One dimension below ten nanometers gives a quantum well.
Two dimensions below ten: a quantum wire.
All three below ten: a quantum dot, the smallest particle scientists have made.
Here is the whole table.
One small dimension: a nano film, two-D, or a quantum well. Two small dimensions: a nanowire, one-D, or a quantum wire. Three small dimensions: a nanoparticle, zero-D, or a quantum dot.
Now the trap. Two-D does not mean two nano dimensions. It means two large dimensions, and only one nano dimension.
And there is no three-D nanomaterial. If nothing is below one hundred nanometers, it is simply bulk.
A quantum material has at least one dimension between one and ten nanometers.
One to ten sits inside one to one hundred. So every quantum material is also a nanomaterial.
But is every nanomaterial a quantum material? No. A fifty nanometer particle is nano, but not quantum. He called this a good midterm question.
One last point. In mathematics, nano size means anything below one thousand nanometers. In materials, only one to one hundred counts, because that is where the properties change.
